newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Berisha acknowledges investors' despair.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Berisha acknowledges investors' despair.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha acknowledged on Friday that many people were in despair over the collapse of pyramid investment schemes but said calm would return once investors knew they would get some money back.
Two-thirds of the money invested in two pyramid schemes had been frozen in state banks and this sum would gradually be returned, he said.
"I won't deny there is a slight financial fever in the country...People are in despair for their money and they are right," Berisha told Reuters and the BBC in an interview.
"But...we have promised to the investors all the frozen money which is in our banks. There is two-thirds of the money there so they will get the majority of their money back," he said.

At least six other nationwide private investment schemes still in operation are paying back interest but not capital and Berisha said negotiations had begun with operators to try to find a solution to overcome their difficulties.
He did not refer to one failed scheme run by a gypsy woman which went bankrupt owing $60 million to some 100,000 depositors.
Thousands of Albanians, faced with the loss of their savings, have staged protests in Tirana and at least 18 other towns around the Balkan state over the past three weeks.

Opposition politicians and a leading member of the ruling right-wing Democratic Party have expressed doubt that the government's pledge would satisfy most Albanians and say the troubles were likely to go on.
"We have never promised full compensation. This could not happen," Berisha said. "We are definitely decided not to provoke inflation." Inflation stood at 17.4 percent in 1996.
The government has said only the poorest people will receive immediate cash in hand, and others will be given savings books or offers to put their investment in shares.
"The money is there, but for technical reasons this money cannot be delivered at once," Berisha said.

The president accused his main political rivals, the Socialists, of funding their campaign in a general election last May on money from pyramid schemes -- the same charge the Socialists level at Berisha's Democratic Party.
The Democrats won the widely-disputed vote, gaining 87 percent of parliamentary seats. The U.S. State Department said in a report that the election process "was deeply flawed".
Berisha said his party's support was confirmed in local elections last October which were described by observers as free and fair.
Asked if he would take advice from some foreign governments to hold a fresh general election as soon as possible, Berisha said: "No."
He said that would only legitimise the boycott by opposition parties.
